title: NRT annotations, #nullable, and compiler warnings (nullable reference types)
hook: Nullable reference types are a conversation between you and the compiler. You mark which references might be null; the compiler warns when your code disagrees. Nothing changes at run time.

blocks.text: **Nullable reference types (NRT)** add `?` to reference types like `string` and `List<T>` so you can express intent: this variable should never be null, or it might be. The compiler tracks **null-state** — whether an expression is *not-null* or *maybe-null* — as it walks your method. When code and annotations disagree, you get warnings in the CS8600 family. These are diagnostics, not runtime checks.

entries.plainDefinition: A C# 8+ feature that annotates reference types with ? and enables compiler warnings about possible null misuse.
entries.example: `string name` means “should not be null”; `string? nickname` means “might be null.”

entries.plainDefinition: Project or file setting that turns annotation and warning contexts on or off.
entries.example: `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` in the .csproj enables both contexts project-wide.

entries.plainDefinition: The compiler’s label for each expression: not-null (safe to dereference) or maybe-null (needs a check).
entries.example: After `if (x is not null)`, x’s null-state becomes not-null inside the block.

entries.plainDefinition: Dereference of a possibly null reference. Means you used `.Length`, `.Count`, etc. while the compiler still sees maybe-null.
entries.example: Fix with a null check, a corrected annotation, or a documented attribute — not `#pragma warning disable`.

blocks.text: Modern .NET project templates enable NRT by default. A warning-clean build means your *source code* matches your intent — it does not mean Redis, JSON deserializers, or third-party libraries cannot still hand you null at run time. Treat NRT as design-time documentation enforced by the compiler, then add runtime guards at process boundaries.

blocks.title: Enable order of operations
blocks.body: 1) Turn on `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` in the project. 2) Fix warnings with real checks and correct `?` annotations. 3) Use `#nullable` pragmas only for legacy file islands. 4) Reach for `!` only when you can prove what the analyzer cannot see.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Read the annotation
items.body: `string` starts as not-null intent. `string?` starts as maybe-null. Unannotated code from older libraries is nullable-oblivious.

items.title: Track assignments
items.body: Assigning a `string?` to a `string` triggers CS8600/CS8601. The compiler sees a maybe-null value going into a not-null slot.

items.title: Apply flow analysis
items.body: `if (x is not null)`, `?.`, `??`, and `ThrowIfNull` update null-state so later dereferences are safe.

items.title: Warn on mismatch
items.body: Dereferencing while maybe-null gives CS8602. The fix is always: change the annotation, add a check, or teach the analyzer with an attribute.

diagram.title: NRT warning pipeline
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  A[Project Nullable enable] --> B[Annotate string vs string?]
  B --> C[Flow analysis per method]
  C --> D{Code matches annotation?}
  D -->|yes| E[Clean build]
  D -->|no| F[CS8600 family warnings]
  F --> G[Fix: check / ? / attribute]

snippet.label: Project switch and file pragma
snippet.explanation: Line comment: project-wide enable is the primary switch. Line 4: file-level `#nullable enable` for mixed migrations. Lines 8–9: disable/restore wraps legacy code without turning warnings off for the whole project.

snippet.label: Redis cache lookup with annotations
snippet.explanation: Line 1: return type `string?` models a cache miss. Line 4: explicit null on miss. Line 7: `is not null` narrows null-state — no warning on `.Length`.

snippet.label: Avoid null! initialization smell
snippet.explanation: Line 4: `null!` tells the compiler “trust me” with no guarantee. Lines 9–11: `required` forces callers to supply `Connection` in an object initializer — a real contract.

blocks.title: NRT vs TypeScript strictNullChecks
rows: No direct pragma; split files or use `@ts-nocheck`

blocks.title: Trusting nullable-oblivious library returns
blocks.body: Older Redis, AWS, or JSON APIs may return plain `string` without `?`. The compiler treats them as oblivious — not guaranteed non-null. Validate at the boundary anyway.

blocks.title: Sprinkling null! to green the build
blocks.body: Every `null!` is a promise you must keep at run time. A project full of them is a map of future NullReferenceException pages.

interviewTakeaways: `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` is the project-wide switch; `#nullable` is per-file.
Warnings encode mismatched intent, not a runtime null ban.
`if (x is not null)` narrows null-state; the compiler does not track across unannotated helpers.
commonPitfalls: Leaving a library nullable-oblivious and trusting its `string` return as non-null.
Initializing every field with `null!` to make the build green.
Dereferencing SQS Message.Body without a check because AWS types were annotated loosely.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript `strictNullChecks` is the closest analogue to `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`. Both are compiler modes, not runtime checks.
